Git's porcelain commands that create new objects periodically check whether the repository has grown substantially since the last maintenance, and if so they invoke `git gc --auto` behind the scenes.

citations.quote: When common porcelain operations that create objects are run, they will check whether the repository has grown substantially since the last maintenance, and if so run git gc automatically.

claims.claim_text: The automatic run is triggered by two thresholds: `gc.auto` (default roughly 6700 loose objects, past which loose objects get packed) and `gc.autoPackLimit` (default 50 packs not marked with a `*.keep` file, past which packs get consolidated into one larger pack), and setting `gc.auto` to 0 disables the whole mechanism, as does setting `gc.autoPackLimit` to 0 for the pack-consolidation part.
Because `gc.autoDetach` defaults to true, the auto run returns immediately and continues in the background on systems that support it, acting as a fallback when `maintenance.autoDetach` isn't set.

When gc actually runs, it prunes unreachable loose objects older than a grace period—by default `prune --expire 2.weeks.ago`, plus `repack --cruft --cruft-expiration 2.weeks.ago` if cruft packs are enabled—which you can override with `gc.pruneExpire` using "now" to prune immediately or "never" to suppress pruning entirely.

It is deliberately conservative about deletion, keeping anything referenced by branches, tags, the index, remote-tracking branches, reflogs, and anything else under `refs/*`, though note that a `git notes` annotation does not keep its object alive, and reflog entries themselves eventually expire (90 days by default, 30 days for entries unreachable from the current tip).

The main risk is running gc concurrently with another process writing to the repository: gc may delete an object that process created but hasn't yet referenced, which can make that process fail or even corrupt the repository if it later adds a reference to the deleted object.

The two-week grace period is specifically designed to mitigate this, so using `--prune=now` significantly raises the danger, and while Git has additional mitigating features, they are not a complete solution—concurrent users must accept a small (though low in practice) risk of corruption.
